Chilcotin (Tŝilhqot'in)

This broader Tŝilhqot’in route introduces a National Government language plan, a particular Xeni Gwet’in caretaker-area account, and a collaboratively produced discussion of salmon stewardship after the 2024 landslide. Individual communities and attributed experiences remain distinct.

01

Identity and context

Tŝilhqot’in is a people’s own name used alongside Chilcotin. Tŝilhqot’in institutions connect language, history and territory.

Read the sources [1] Tŝilhqot’in National Government

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Community governments, language and territorial histories. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] Tŝilhqot’in National Government [2] Tŝilhqot’in National Government [3] tsilhqotinlanguage.ca

03

A plan for language work

The 2026 plan organizes language work around teaching and immersion, intergenerational learning, resources and coordinated governance. It links these directions with an earlier strategy. The listed actions express intended work; they do not establish that every programme has been delivered or that all learning outcomes were achieved.

Read the sources [4] Tŝilhqot’in National Government

04

One caretaker-area history within the broader Nation

The Nemiah Valley account identifies a particular Xeni Gwet’in caretaker area between Chilko and Taseko lakes. It recounts opposition to proposed development and attributes personal interpretation. This is one community/place history, not a substitute for every Tŝilhqot’in community’s account.

Read the sources [5] Tŝilhqot’in National Government; page updated August 2026

05

Salmon and a changing landscape

The 2025 report connects Chilko Lake sockeye with community concerns after the 2024 landslide. It presents stewardship as a response to changing waters and cumulative pressures. The 2011 aerial lake photograph predates that event; it is not a view of the slide, proof of habitat recovery or a fisheries forecast.

Read the sources [6] Tŝilhqot’in Nation with researchers at UBC and York University
